content.title: Trust Me: The False Prophet (TV Mini Series 2026) ⭐ 7.8 | Documentary
content.text: Episodes4Videos1PhotosFeatured reviewsA Courageous Story of Heroes and SurvivorsAs someone that was born into fundamentalist religion, I've always been interested in documentaries like Keep Sweet and Obey... when Trust Me came out, I knew I had to watch. I had no idea what I was in for...This is a firsthand documentary account of the takedown of a pedophilic cult leader, from the inside, by one heroic woman's insistence and devotion to protecting other girls and women survivors. And it is truly amazing. I was not prepared for the ending, or the tears I would be reduced to. I recommend this as a must watch for everyone who may be interested in this topic.False prophets and cult leaders may seem like a thing of the distant past but they are alive and well, and left unchecked they will harm the most innocent among us in the most despicable ways. Rarely do we see them and those connected to them held responsible like has happened in this case, but that makes this documentary all the more valuable as an example of what is possible. I'm so proud of Christine, of Julia, of Naomi, and of these girls. I hope their joy for life and freedom to only build going forward. There is hope, life goes on!Sam the DevilA deeply frustrating watch. It's heartbreaking to see the level of brainwashing and trauma inflicted on women and children within these secluded communities. This documentary serves as yet another grim case study of how a deluded, powerful man can exploit the vulnerable. Furthermore, it highlights the staggering inadequacy of government intervention, which often allows these situations to fester for years. These stories are chilling reminders that one person's ego can derail the lives of entire generations. I sincerely hope every woman and child featured can find a path toward recovery and peace.Thought provoking viewing.Following the imprisonment of leader Warren Jeffs, cult expert Christine Marie and her husband Tolga travel to the insular community of Short Creek to document the human side of the FLDS. They quickly encounter Samuel Bateman, a self-proclaimed prophet who has established a breakaway group built on his own deviant fantasies and a claim to divine authority. Over several months, the pair record thousands of hours of undercover footage, capturing the exploitation of Bateman's numerous wives and children."Trust Me: The False Prophet" is a harrowing and deeply unsettling series that benefits from being filmed in near real-time. The behaviour on display is so alien that it feels like another planet, let alone another country, with a level of dehumanisation that is difficult to fathom. Women are stripped of their names and referred to by numbers, functioning as little more than a subservient, free labour force for Bateman's network of businesses. It is a repellant look at how the name of God is used as a smokescreen for a predatory narcissist to exert total sex and control over the vulnerable.The documentary is expertly crafted, providing a vital distinction between the main FLDS community and Bateman's warped breakaway cult. The inclusion of figures like Naomi is particularly powerful; her evolution from a brainwashed defender to a courageous witness provides a necessary layer of hope. It is tragic to see how the children's lives were disrupted by Bateman's abhorrent behaviour, but the series does a fine job of highlighting the resilience of those who finally found their voice. Even the most bizarre elements, like Bateman's delusional attempt to invite the late Queen Elizabeth II to his home, are handled with a critical yet fair lens.Christine Marie emerges as a remarkable and fiercely brave figure throughout the ordeal. Her ability to maintain a façade of devotion while coaching Bateman into his own trap is a masterclass in tension, especially during the claustrophobic car sequences where she must mask her utter horror. The moment she and Tolga realise their cover has been blown is as gripping as any scripted thriller. Netflix has delivered a robust and thought-provoking series that avoids cheap sensationalism, instead providing a gritty account of how logic can be surrendered to a man with a massive ego and no moral compass.8/10.The Prophet Drives a Bentley. The Wives Sew Their Own Dresses.Trust Me: The False Prophet is one of the most compelling docuseries I've seen in a long time. It is powerful, beautifully filmed, heartbreaking, and ultimately hopeful, a rare combination that stays with you long after the final episode.What makes this series particularly striking is watching, in real time, how Sam Bateman systematically dismantled the very belief system he claimed to represent. These women and children surrendered everything: their autonomy, their identities, their futures, to a man who convinced them he spoke directly to God.Meanwhile, they were sewing their own matching handmade dresses while he was driving a Bentley. The cognitive dissonance was genuinely tragic.The manipulation on display is textbook, and I mean that literally. Isolation, manufactured dependency, intermittent reinforcement, identity reconstruction. Watching it unfold through the eyes of the survivors is both an education in coercive control and a complete gut punch.Christine Marie is the quiet center of this story, and she is extraordinary. There is something almost unbearable about watching her methodically, compassionately work to crack open the armor of women who had every reason to protect the man who hurt them while trying to stay strong inside.The moment when loyalty begins to fracture, when you can see a woman start to recognize that love was the weapon used against her, that is documentary filmmaking at its finest.This series doesn't just tell a story. It bears witness.CourageousHaving grown up in Utah and witnessing these types of polygamous families I can see how Christine wanted to help!This is a powerful documentary and very well done, with respect to the women and girls who have been born into a very harmful religious system.This show, among so many others, is one more example of how a powerful and deluded man can be take control of a community and use a religion for his own evil "kingdom".Christine and Tolga took the time to make connections with this community to save other humans dignity and bring justice to victims.These stories are chilling reminders that the past (and sadly present) teachings of "religious" leaders can damage generations of women, children and even the men within those communities and in patriarchy societies.Thank you for having the courage to make this film! I hope more of the girls and women will begin to understand what brainwashing happened to them and begin to heal!More like thisRelated interestsDid you knowEverything New on Netflix in AprilEverything New on Netflix in April"XO, Kitty" returns for Season 3.
